newsitem.title: UK: Top British Liberals back Blair-led coalition idea.
newsitem.headline: Top British Liberals back Blair-led coalition idea.

text.p: Two senior members of Britain's Liberal Democrats on Monday publicly called for a post-election coalition with the Labour Party, heaping pressure on party leader Paddy Ashdown to back the idea.
Foreign affairs spokesman Menzies Campbell and elder statesman Lord Bill Rodgers said the Liberals should accept any invitation from Labour leader Tony Blair to become ministers in his government.
Earlier, Ashdown said he believed a coalition with Labour was possible, but unlikely, in the event of a so-called "hung parliament" in which no party had a majority of seats.

A coalition government, which would be Britain's first since World War Two, is likely only if Labour, at present 20 points ahead of the Conservatives in the opinion polls, wins the election without gaining an overall majority in parliament.

Commenting on the prospect of a government of the two parties, Labour's chief parliamentary business manager Donald Dewar told BBC radio: "We will cross that bridge if we come to it. We don't anticipate being in that situation."

But Rodgers, a former Labour minister who left the party in the 1980s after a leftward policy lurch, told a fringe meeting at the Liberals' annual conference: "If the opportunity occurs...we should be prepared to play our part in government."
He added: "It would be good for Britain if to the weight of Labour was added the radicalism of the Liberal Democrats."

Campbell told the same meeting: "If in order to keep the Conservatives out of Downing Street (government) it is necessary to enter into arrangements with the Labour Party, I personally am happy to contemplate such an arrangement.
"But its purpose would be to ensure the prevailing of Liberal Democrat policies."
Neither Rodgers nor Campbell went as far as another Liberal Democrat legislator, Alex Carlile, who said on Sunday that one day Labour and the Liberals might merge into a single party.
Ashdown told BBC radio: "All the options are open. To coin a phrase, nothing is ruled in, nothing is ruled out.
"Is it possible we will do what you suggest? Yes. Is it likely viewed from the moment? No," he said.
Party president Robert Maclennan told the conference the Liberals should concentrate their fire on the Conservatives, who had "hardened in office into ugly authoritarian arrogance".
"There is one thing that our two parties (Labour and the Liberals) have in common," Maclennan, also a former Labour minister, told the conference. "We are not the Conservatives.
"And so between us and Labour this is not the time for poison blowpipes or battle axes."
But treasury spokesman Malcolm Bruce said if Labour came out against a single European currency, as financial markets seemed to expect, "we are bound to have a pretty fundamental disagreement".
The Liberals are the only major British party to have committed themselves to entering a single currency provided Britain meets the economic criteria for doing so.

Blair has moved Labour away from many of its old socialist stances and towards some traditional Liberal policies such as constitutional reform, winning converts from other parties ahead of a general election due by next May.
The Liberals currently stand at about 14 percent in the polls. However, impressive successes in local government polls since the 1992 general election have buoyed activists' spirits.
